findings.title: Background legacy writes inherit the request context
findings.body: `WithTimeoutCause` creates a child of the incoming request context; it does not detach cancellation. The API server cancels that context when the request handler returns, which happens immediately after this method returns, so the legacy write can be canceled before it completes. The same pattern is used for delete, update, and delete-collection at lines 110, 135, and 163. The unified write is still reported as successful, leaving legacy storage unsynchronized.

findings.title: Legacy updates are recomputed against a potentially divergent object
findings.body: The legacy update receives the original `objInfo`, so it computes the update independently against the legacy object's current state. During dual writing, that state can differ from unified storage; patches, defaults, or other update logic can therefore produce a legacy object different from the object successfully written to unified storage. The previous implementation passed the unified update result to legacy through an update wrapper, avoiding this divergence.

findings.title: Independent goroutines can apply mutations to legacy out of order
findings.body: Every successful mutation starts an independent goroutine, with no per-resource ordering or queue. For example, a delete can reach legacy before an earlier create, return not found, and then the delayed create can leave the supposedly deleted object in legacy; an update can similarly arrive before its create. These legacy errors are not retried, so the stores can remain divergent.

findings.title: Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy writes
findings.body: The asynchronous writes are not tracked, but `Destroy` immediately destroys both backends. If shutdown calls `Destroy` while a legacy write is still running, the backend can be closed underneath that write and the shadow write can be lost. Track and drain pending writes, or otherwise ensure the legacy backend remains available until they finish.

findings.title: Write latency and error metrics are attributed to the wrong backend
findings.body: When unified storage fails, this records a legacy duration even though legacy storage was never called; the same mistake occurs for update at line 129. Conversely, the asynchronous legacy delete-collection result at line 166 is recorded as a storage duration. This misattributes backend errors and latency, leaving the corresponding storage or legacy metrics inaccurate.

findings.title: Delete metrics use each object name as the kind label
findings.body: This call passes `name` where the other duration-recording calls pass the resource kind (`options.Kind`). If the value is used as the metrics kind label, every distinct deleted object creates a separate Prometheus time series, causing unbounded cardinality as objects are deleted and making per-kind metrics inaccurate.
